newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans' doubts mount over Waigel tax reform bid.
newsitem.headline: Germans' doubts mount over Waigel tax reform bid.

text.p: As Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reform plan takes shape, scepticism among Germans about whether he will meet tax-cutting promises has hit a new high, a leading polling group said on Wednesday.
Waigel's tax strategy, centrepiece of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's bid for a record fifth election win in 1998, boldly aims to slice 30 billion marks ($19 billion) off the national tax burden.

But wrangling in Kohl's coalition over slashing income taxes, along with a deal to raise value added tax to offset the cuts partly, has dashed hopes among ordinary Germans that they will profit in the end, the Allensbach institute said.
A survey by the institute found that 53 percent of Germans thought the reform -- to take effect mainly in 1999 -- would only redistribute taxes. Only 13 percent actually expected cuts.
"A majority of Germans think that the planned tax reform is above all about raising VAT," the institute's Renate Koecher wrote in the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper.
A tax policy working group chaired by Waigel is due to complete its work next week, and is nearing a compromise on how to reshape income taxes.
Under two models being discussed, the top income tax rate would fall to 39 percent from 53 percent.
Waigel favours a sliding scale starting at 19 percent, down from 26 percent, while coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) support a stepped scheme starting at 10 percent.
Corporation tax would fall to 35 percent from 45 percent.
Kohl will lead a round of coalition talks on Thursday to thrash out details of the tax package, as well as address plans to reform Germany's struggling compulsory pensions scheme.
Also on the agenda will be whether to use the VAT tax hike to ease high German labour costs, seen as one reason for a jobs flight abroad which has pushed unemployment to post-war records.

Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who can block some tax measures through their control of the upper house of parliament, have flatly rejected a VAT rise to finance a cut in the top rate of income tax.
Germans show no sign of backing the reform due to the income tax cuts. Instead the coalition debate over scrapping myriad tax breaks has topped the evening television news programmes.

A one-point increase in the 15 percent rate of VAT, proposals to tax life insurance, pensions and jobless benefits, as well as profits on share dealings have also stirred a hostile response from powerful special interests.
"The Bonn government has succeeded in destroying any confidence people might have had in the wisdom of the reforms," the heavyweight Handelsblatt daily wrote.
"Step by step, the milestones set last autumn in the new tax system have been dug up and put in the store room."
Kohl has said that consultations over the tax plan were likely to last all year, but Germany may not have the luxury of spending so much time putting its financial house in order.

Handicapped by unemployment at nearly 11 percent and tax revenues falling short of target, Waigel will be hard pushed to cut state borrowing and meet his goal of qualifying this year for planned European monetary union in 1999.

Former Bundesbank President Karl Otto Poehl on Tuesday became the latest pundit to cast doubt on whether Germany can cut its budget deficit below the Maastricht ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product in 1997.

"Without a considerable acceleration of economic growth, Germany will fail to meet the deficit criteria," Poehl said in Paris. Bonn's insistence on a strict interpretation of the treaty made the situation "a little ugly", he said.
